strengths: Principled theoretical contribution: Proposition 1 elegantly unifies training-free guidance with Langevin MCMC, providing theoretical justification for the proposed local search strategy
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (planning, offline RL, image generation) demonstrates the breadth and generality of the framework
Practical efficiency gains clearly demonstrated: 2x compute savings in image generation, >90% success rates with global search on planning tasks, competitive performance on D4RL
Well-executed technical framework combining classical search algorithms (BFS/DFS) with diffusion model sampling in an intuitive and effective way
Excellent presentation with clear figures, detailed algorithms, comprehensive appendices, and thorough experimental protocols supporting reproducibility
Addresses an important and timely problem (inference-time control of diffusion models) with practical solutions showing consistent improvements
weaknesses: Limited novelty: individual components (Langevin MCMC, BFS/DFS, training-free guidance) are existing techniques; the contribution is primarily in their combination
Task-specific verifier requirement significantly limits generality; each domain requires custom-designed verifier functions without principled design guidelines
Theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) establishes only continuous-limit equivalence; practical applicability with discrete implementations is unclear
Insufficient analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity; multiple hyperparameters require careful tuning (Table 3) without clear adaptive tuning methodology despite claims
Marginal improvements on several benchmarks, particularly in D4RL (Table 1) where improvements are often modest, raising questions about practical significance
Incomplete analysis of when each search strategy (local/global, BFS/DFS) is beneficial and missing systematic study of compute-quality trade-offs
Limited comparison with recent inference-time scaling methods; primarily compared with simple Best-of-N baseline for image generation
Verifier design details and hacking/adversarial robustness concerns are not adequately addressed; limited discussion of failure modes

strengths: Systematic elucidation of BFS design space (tempering, scoring, resampling) with clear takeaways; prior methods shown to be special cases of unified framework
Novel adaptive DFS algorithm with threshold-based compute allocation demonstrating 2× efficiency gains without prior difficulty knowledge
Rigorous theoretical contribution establishing equivalence between training-free guidance and annealed Langevin MCMC (Proposition 1) with convergence bounds (Theorem 1)
Comprehensive experiments across multiple domains (text-to-image, planning, offline RL) with thorough ablations and reproducibility details in appendices
Clear demonstration of joint scaling benefits over scaling global/local search independently (Figure 4), establishing improved Pareto frontiers
Practical double-verifier strategy for mitigating reward hacking with substantial improvements (FID 155.7→127.8 on ImageNet)
Strong consistent empirical results: improved BFS outperforms prior methods; policy distillation competitive with online RL while significantly faster
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: BFS/DFS for diffusion established in prior SMC/tree search work; improved design combines existing techniques (Increase tempering from DAS, Max scoring from FK-steering, SSP resampling from DAS); Langevin MCMC for compositional generation from Du et al. 2023

Significant gap between theory and practice: Proposition 1 equivalence holds only for T→∞ limit; practical finite-T approximation quality unexplored. Theorem 1 assumes bounded support, strong log-concavity, L-smoothness—unrealistic for complex multimodal distributions; bounds loose with limited actionable guidance

Experimental concerns: BFS ablation improvements often modest/within error bars (Table 1 differences <0.05); unfair baseline comparisons in D4RL where TFG/DAS get 2× compute; when equalized, advantages diminish (Medium HalfCheetah: DAS 53.4 vs TTS 54.8)
Insufficient analysis of when/why joint scaling outperforms proportional allocation—no theoretical characterization or intuitive explanation of compute tradeoffs

Extensive hyperparameter complexity undermines practicality claim: requires tuning τ_t, scoring function, Nrecur, ρ, µ, δ_t, ∆T; Tables 8-9 show substantial sensitivity (performance varies within/near error bars); contradicts 'principled' classical search appeal

DFS design choices lack principled justification: backtracking depth ∆T≥T/4 appears arbitrary; limited ablation on threshold schedule δ_t; concurrent work ABCD claims better sample quality through full denoising but advantages unclear

Limited failure mode analysis: no discussion of when DFS underperforms BFS or guidance for practitioners on method selection; missing comparisons with other search strategies (evolutionary search, MCTS variants)

strengths: Well-motivated unified framework combining global and local search with principled theoretical grounding via Proposition 1 and Theorem 1
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse domains (text-to-image, planning, offline RL) with extensive ablations and implementation details
Adaptive compute allocation in DFS that dynamically adjusts based on instance difficulty without requiring advance knowledge, showing up to 2× compute reduction
Novel theoretical connection unifying annealed Langevin MCMC and training-free guidance with recurrence, providing convergence analysis
Improved BFS design that clarifies and unifies prior work (SVDD, DAS, FK-steering) within a coherent framework
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components: BFS improvements over baselines are modest (~3-5%, Table 2) and sometimes within overlapping error bars; local search largely builds on Du et al. (2023); primary contribution is the combination rather than new algorithmic insights

Significant theoretical limitations: Proposition 1 only holds 'in the continuous limit where T→∞' without characterizing approximation quality for practical finite T; Theorem 1's convergence bound has unclear practical implications with dense exponential terms and assumptions (strong log-concavity) that may not hold for multimodal distributions

Questionable experimental fairness: Offline RL allows baselines twice the compute; compute/NFE accounting differs across methods; modest improvements often within error bars (e.g., Table 3) without statistical significance testing; no direct comparison with concurrent work (ABCD, EvoSearch)

Substantial hyperparameter complexity poorly addressed: Method requires tuning tempering schedule, scoring function, resampling method, backtracking depth, threshold schedule, guidance strength (ρ̄, μ̄), and verifier choice; Section 6 dismisses this as 'potential limitation' despite Tables 7-8 showing significant sensitivity; no clear guidance for new domains

DFS relies on strong assumptions about verifier calibration and comparability across noise levels; no analysis of robustness to miscalibrated or adversarial verifiers, particularly Q-functions that don't form valid probability distributions
Double-verifier strategy is orthogonal contribution evaluated in only one experiment; unclear how much improvement comes from inference-time scaling versus using two classifiers

Missing empirical comparisons with acknowledged concurrent work (ABCD, EvoSearch); incomplete offline RL evaluation (no DFS results); policy distillation setup differs from baseline making comparison unclear

Reproducibility concerns: Complex hyperparameter tuning, no code release mentioned, and many task-specific design choices (e.g., evaluation steps S vary by task) limit reproducibility and generalization

strengths: Comprehensive unified framework combining global search (BFS/DFS) and local search (Langevin MCMC) with elegant theoretical grounding (Proposition 1, Theorem 1)
Exceptional experimental breadth across four distinct domains (text-to-image, planning, offline RL, policy distillation) with consistent improvements over strong baselines
Thorough ablation studies clearly elucidate design space (tempering, scoring, resampling) and provide improved BFS design beating DAS/FK-steering/SVDD/TreeG
Novel adaptive DFS algorithm with backtracking enables compute allocation based on instance difficulty without prior knowledge
Strong theoretical contribution unifying training-free guidance with recurrence to annealed Langevin MCMC with rigorous convergence analysis
Practical contributions including double-verifier strategy for mitigating reward hacking and offline policy distillation results
Exceptional rigor with extensive appendices providing detailed proofs, algorithms, and experimental specifications supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty—core components (BFS/DFS, Langevin MCMC, training-free guidance) are established; main contribution is skillful engineering and combination rather than novel algorithmic or theoretical insights

Hyperparameter proliferation (threshold δₜ, backtracking depth ∆T, tempering τₜ, scoring functions, resampling, local search steps, guidance strength ρ/µ) with significant sensitivity demonstrated (Table 8: 42.5±5.2 to 48.1±1.1 across configurations); acknowledged as limitation but substantial practical concern

Theoretical results require strong unjustified assumptions: Proposition 1 needs T→∞ (idealization for finite-step diffusion); Theorem 1 assumes α-strongly log-concave and L-log-smooth distributions with bounded support unlikely to hold for complex distributions; gap between asymptotic theory and finite-step practice not addressed

Efficiency analysis incomplete: only NFE comparisons provided without wall-clock time comparisons despite 1000+ GPU hours used; memory overhead (buffers in DFS, particle management) not discussed; actual runtime savings unclear

Evaluation limitations: Image generation only compared with recent tree-search methods; offline RL baselines unfairly allowed 2× compute; D4RL shows comparable not superior performance to QGPO; policy distillation compared only to DPPO

Incremental empirical improvements on ablations: Max vs. Difference scoring shows 1.032 vs 1.013 (Table 1, within noise); Increase vs. Constant tempering 1.087 vs 1.032 (modest gains lack deeper insight)
Limited analysis of problem characteristics determining when global vs. local search dominates; no characterization of failure modes or method limitations
Hyperparameter search appears critical (Table 9 shows search-set vs. eval-set gap: 94.3 vs 93.9) but details lacking; reproducibility concerns despite extensive appendices
